title: Eratosthenes sized up the whole Earth from a stick’s shadow
body: At noon on the summer solstice, a vertical stick at Syene (today’s Aswan) cast no shadow, while at Alexandria, to the north, a stick’s shadow put the Sun about 7.2 degrees from overhead: one-fiftieth of a full circle. Because sunlight arrives in nearly parallel rays, the same angle separates the two cities at the Earth’s centre, so the roughly 5,000 stadia between them is 1/50 of the way round: 250,000 stadia in all. How close that comes is still debated, because nobody knows exactly how long his stadion was; depending on the length assumed, and on whether you take 250,000 or the 252,000 that Pliny reports, the result is within about 2.4% of the truth or 10 to 15% too big. His own book is lost, and the method reaches us through a simplified retelling by the later writer Cleomedes.

slides.alt: Animation on papyrus: at noon a stick at Syene casts no shadow while one at Alexandria casts a 7.2° shadow. Parallel sun rays carry the angle to Earth’s centre, 50 copies of the 5,000-stadia arc make 250,000 stadia, and a scale compares the result with 40,008 km.

slides.prompt: Line your angle up with the noon shadow of Alexandria’s stick, while the Sun stands overhead at Syene (today’s Aswan). How big is the Earth?
slides.takeaway: The shadow’s 7.2° is a fiftieth of a circle, so the Earth is 50 times the 5,000 stadia to Syene: 250,000 stadia, about 39,000 to 46,000 km by the stadion, against 40,008 km.

slides.heading: Known only second-hand
slides.text: Eratosthenes’ own book, *On the Measure of the Earth*, is lost. His method survives only through later writers, above all a simplified version by Cleomedes, and the famous detail of sunlight shining straight down a well at Syene also reaches us only through such later accounts.

left.label: Cleomedes’ version
left.text: Syene sits exactly on the Tropic of Cancer and due south of Alexandria, so the noon Sun on the solstice is straight overhead.

right.label: In reality
right.text: Syene lies a little north of the Tropic, by less than a degree, and about 3 degrees of longitude east of Alexandria.

slides.question: Why does the shadow angle at Alexandria match the angle between the two cities at the Earth’s centre?
options: The Sun was overhead at Alexandria
slides.explanation: With parallel rays, the ray at Alexandria and the vertical at Syene are parallel lines, so the line from Alexandria to the centre crosses both at the same angle.

slides.label: stadia: the figure the Roman writer Pliny gives for Eratosthenes’ Earth
slides.text: Unlike 250,000, it divides evenly by every whole number from 1 to 10, which may be no accident. Historians disagree about why the figure changed.

slides.clue: The Greek name for an upright rod whose shadow shows the Sun’s angle, as on a sundial
slides.detail: From a Greek word meaning “one that knows or examines”. It is also the name for the part of a sundial that casts the shadow.
